en: Theravāda Vinaya Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
Ārāmavagga 54.
The Training Rule on Being Invited to Eat.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a certain brahmin invited some bhikkhunīs and fed them.
After the bhikkhunīs had finished eating and were satisfied, they went to their relatives' homes; some ate there, while others took almsfood and departed.
Then that brahmin said this to his neighbors:
“The nuns have been satisfied by me, noble sirs; come, I shall satisfy you as well.
They replied, “What, noble sir, will you satisfy us?”
“Those who were invited by her also came to our houses; some ate there, while others took almsfood and departed.
Then that brahmin complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“How can these bhikkhunīs, having eaten in our house, eat elsewhere? And I am not capable of giving as much as they require!”
The bhikkhunīs heard that brahmin complaining, grumbling, and making a scene.
Those bhikkhunīs who were of few desires... [and so forth]... complained, grumbled, and made a scene, saying:
"How can these bhikkhunīs eat otherwise than after they have finished their meal and been invited to desist?"... [and so forth]...
“Is it true, monks, that nuns, having finished their meal and being invited to desist, are eating elsewhere?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them... [as before]...
“How indeed, monks, can bhikkhunīs, having finished their meal and being invited to stop, eat otherwise?
This, monks, is neither for the pleasing of those without confidence nor for the increase of those with confidence.
… And so, monks, let the bhikkhunīs recite this training rule:”
“Whatever nun, having been invited or having been offered food, should eat or consume either solid food or soft food, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
“Whatever nun” means whichever nun of such a kind... [and so forth].
"A bhikkhunī" ...
[as before] ... this is the kind of bhikkhunī intended in this context.
"Invited" means:
"Invited with one of the five kinds of cooked food": here,
"having been invited" means that food is visible, the meal is visible, [the donor] offers it while standing within arm's reach, and a refusal is visible.
"Hard food" (khādanīya) means:
setting aside the five kinds of cooked food, rice gruel, that which is to be taken within a watch of the night, that which is to be taken for seven days, and that which is to be taken for life,
the remainder is called "hard food."
“Eatable” means the five kinds of cooked food: boiled rice, sour gruel, flour, fish, and meat.
If one receives it with the thought, “I will chew it” or “I will eat it,” there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For every mouthful, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one who has been invited, perceiving that he has been invited, eats or consumes solid food or soft food, there is an offense of expiation.
If one who has been invited, being in doubt, eats or consumes solid food or soft food, there is an offense of expiation.
If one who has been invited perceives that they have not been invited, and eats or consumes either soft food or solid food, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

If one accepts for the purpose of food anything that is to be taken at the proper time, or for seven days, or for as long as life lasts, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). For every swallow, there is an offense of wrong-doing... [etc. ... *Note: The term "animantitasaññā" is translated as "perceives that they have not been invited. The phrase "yāmakālikaṁ sattāhakālikaṁ yāvajīvikaṁ āhāratthāya paṭiggaṇhāti" refers to accepting medicinal substances intended for consumption during the day, for seven days, or for life, when used as food.*
There is no offense if she is invited but not formally requested [to eat more],
and she drinks rice-gruel.
If she eats after having obtained permission from the owner;
if she uses post-midnight, seven-day, or lifetime medicines when there is a legitimate reason;
or if she is insane.
"For one who is a first offender":
thus ends the fourth training rule.
